sentences: Aethra reported Evadne’s death and Iphis’s loss after the funeral. This source event belongs to the account the traveler heard.

Aethra tells Vale the funeral’s further loss. Evadne died at Capaneus’s pyre despite Iphis’s plea. He has lost both his children. The surviving children carry ashes and speak of vengeance. Aethra recalls the play’s closing oath: Argos owes Athens aid, while Athena names another war for the children. Iphis comes to sit beside the shrine steps.

After the witnessed appeal, {actor} uses the prepared grave, cloth and tools to bury Ajax. The vigil closes with actual burial in the named Trojan account.
Ajax must not lie unburied, and Odysseus should speak for his burial.
Antigone cleans the dust from her brother and anoints him.
Antigone covers her brother with earth and leaves the raven feather on the mound.
Antigone draws the black cloth over her brother and lays a raven feather on it.
Before Teucer and Odysseus, {actor} hears the witnessed appeal receive support. The vigil can become a rite. Ajax still awaits actual burial at the grave.
Creon names the road to the palace at Mycenae.
Dione names the farm that gave Electra shelter.
Dione reads Teucer’s account of Ajax’s public burial.
Dione reads Teucer’s account of the household burial.
Dione reads Teucer’s account of the witnessed burial.
Dione’s table holds the herald’s truce, the funeral account, Myrine’s signed list and the refuge tablet. Vale sits with her. Dione sets the bread between them. The new verses join the earlier song.

Dione’s table holds the herald’s truce, the funeral account, Myrine’s signed list and the refuge tablet. {actor} sits with her. Dione sets the bread between them. The new verses join the earlier song.
Electra lives in a poor farmer's house in the Argive countryside, far from the palace.
Electra met her brother at Agamemnon's tomb while she brought offerings.
Electra names what her family has lost.
Electra waited outside the Mycenaean palace for her brother to come home.
Helen sailed home from Troy herself, and no phantom ever stood in her place.
Helen spent the war in Egypt, and only a phantom of her went to Troy.
Helen tells her own account.
Helen waited out the war in Egypt while a phantom took her place at Troy.
Helen went to Troy with Paris and stayed there through the war.

In the tale, an oracle demanded a noble maiden’s life. Demophon refused to compel a household. Heracles’s daughter offered herself for her siblings and rejected a lottery. The keeper gives her reasons their full place, then names the life the city’s safety cost. Vale listens.

In this adapted telling, the herald confirmed a witnessed return of the Argive dead under a burial truce.
Ismene names the road to Agamemnon’s tomb.
Its bearer speaks for the house of Oedipus in mourning.
Myrine agreed at Eleusis to walk along the shore path to Piraeus with a traveler from this company. Her departure needs their company.
Myrine arrived at Piraeus, held her household’s basket and signed her own account on the return list. Thaleia kept the listed household’s place.

Myrine names the household she represents. She agrees to walk from Eleusis to Piraeus along the shore path with a traveler from Vale’s company. She will wait for company before setting out. At the quay she will claim the care prepared for her household.

Myrine names the household she represents. She agrees to walk from Eleusis to Piraeus along the shore path with a traveler from {actor}’s company. She will wait for company before setting out. At the quay she will claim the care prepared for her household.

Myrine rests at the quay with the basket now in her hands. Thaleia finds her household on the list and keeps its place. Before Vale, Myrine signs the margin: “I reached the quay. My household’s place was kept, and its basket passed to me.” Her words can travel to Dione.

Myrto names the tomb in Egypt where Helen waited.
Myrto points out the Northern Road to Ajax’s camp.
No one may bury or mourn Polynices, who lies outside the city walls.
Odysseus adds his voice to Teucer’s appeal.
Odysseus asks for a public burial.
Odysseus reads Teucer’s plea aloud.
Odysseus supports a public burial for his former rival. {actor} undertakes the work of the rite. The burial still needs cloth, grave tools and earth.
Odysseus tells Vale that the shield belongs with Eurysaces in Tecmessa’s care. This is testimony within the named Trojan account.
Odysseus tells {actor} that the shield belongs with Eurysaces in Tecmessa’s care. This is testimony within the named Trojan account.
Orestes comes home in secret and finds Electra at Agamemnon's tomb.
Orestes comes home to find Electra married to a poor Argive farmer.
Orestes comes home to find Electra waiting outside the Mycenaean palace.
Patroclus steps down onto the quay and makes room beside Vale.
Patroclus steps down onto the quay and makes room beside {actor}.
Polynices’ Shade points beneath the bent olive, where his sister can lay him to rest.
Tecmessa asks for a quiet burial with the household.
Tecmessa asks for a quiet household rite. {actor} agrees to prepare it. Ajax still awaits the cloth, grave tools and earth.
Tecmessa sets Ajax’s shield beside her tent for Eurysaces.
Tecmessa tells Vale that Ajax wanted their son Eurysaces to keep the shield. This is testimony within the named Trojan account.

Teucer asks Vale to carry his written burial plea to Odysseus. He places the plea on the camp bench. This is testimony within the named Trojan account.

Thaleia shows Vale the resting place at the quay. She has cloth for Eleusis, a basket for the homeward meal and a blanket the sailors say was meant for Marathon. She asks for the mothers’ own list before assigning the berth.

The Aeschylus account governs the Atreid household, beginning at Agamemnon’s tomb. The other accounts remain alternative stories.
The Argive mothers ask Athens to win back their sons' bodies from Thebes for burial.
The Chorus Elder names the beach where Helen returned from Troy.
The Egyptian account governs Helen's whereabouts and testimony. The Trojan account remains an alternative story.
The Euripides account governs the Atreid household, beginning at the Argive farmhouse. The other accounts remain alternative stories.
The Sophocles account governs the Atreid household, beginning at the Mycenaean palace. The other accounts remain alternative stories.
The Trojan account governs Helen's whereabouts and testimony. No phantom has been established in this history.

The blanket from Piraeus lies beside the altar. The keeper sets it aside for present-day guests. The old tale continues beside a place made ready for someone who may need it. Vale waits with the keeper.

The guard reads the burial prohibition aloud.
The household of Oedipus may bury Polynices, and the gate guard must let them pass.

The keeper continues the earlier tale. Creon seized Antigone and Ismene to force their father’s return. Theseus brought them back. Polyneices then sought his father’s blessing for war. Oedipus refused and cursed both sons. Vale hears how care and power crossed these paths.

The keeper continues the earlier tale. Creon seized Antigone and Ismene to force their father’s return. Theseus brought them back. Polyneices then sought his father’s blessing for war. Oedipus refused and cursed both sons. {actor} hears how care and power crossed these paths.

The keeper finishes the tale. Oedipus entrusted his final place to Theseus alone. His daughters mourned and returned toward Thebes. Theseus kept the place secret and promised them care. Vale hears the public promise while the old resting place keeps its silence.

The keeper finishes the tale. Oedipus entrusted his final place to Theseus alone. His daughters mourned and returned toward Thebes. Theseus kept the place secret and promised them care. {actor} hears the public promise while the old resting place keeps its silence.

The keeper names an earlier time, before the deaths of the Theban brothers. In Sophocles’s tale, blind Oedipus reaches this grove with Antigone. The townspeople fear his name. Theseus grants him shelter. Vale listens at the present boundary stone.

The keeper names an earlier time, before the deaths of the Theban brothers. In Sophocles’s tale, blind Oedipus reaches this grove with Antigone. The townspeople fear his name. Theseus grants him shelter. {actor} listens at the present boundary stone.

The keeper opens a separate tale after Heracles’s death, under Demophon, son of Theseus. Iolaus and the children sought shelter here. Eurystheus’s herald claimed them and used force. Demophon upheld the altar’s protection. Vale hears the claim beside the present shrine.

The keeper opens a separate tale after Heracles’s death, under Demophon, son of Theseus. Iolaus and the children sought shelter here. Eurystheus’s herald claimed them and used force. Demophon upheld the altar’s protection. {actor} hears the claim beside the present shrine.

The keeper sets out the final dispute. Alcmene demands Eurystheus’s death. The city’s rule protects a prisoner taken alive. Eurystheus defends his choices and foretells his grave’s power. Alcmene orders him away to die. The keeper writes the Marathon record for Vale.

The keeper sets out the final dispute. Alcmene demands Eurystheus’s death. The city’s rule protects a prisoner taken alive. Eurystheus defends his choices and foretells his grave’s power. Alcmene orders him away to die. The keeper writes the Marathon record for {actor}.

The keeper tells the next part. The daughter’s sacrifice preceded the battle. Athens won; Iolaus pursued Eurystheus, who was brought back alive. The messenger distinguished what he saw from the story of Iolaus’s renewed youth. Vale hears the cost before the victory.

The keeper writes on the refuge tablet beside Vale. It records a present custom: hear a stranger’s need, offer rest and seek protection. The old tale gives this promise its weight.

The water cup and honey rest beside the grove. The keeper recalls the gentle offering taught to Oedipus, which Ismene made in the earlier tale. Today’s gift rests at the same boundary for the keeper’s rite. Vale waits beside it.

Thebes gives up the Argive dead to Athens for burial, under witness.

Theseus reads the herald’s return to Vale. In this new telling, both sides accepted the burial truce. The remains reached Eleusis under witness. The mothers now have their dead; their funeral and care still lie before them.

Vale asks Adrastus why the army went to Thebes. He owns the failed expedition and the warning he set aside. Aethra asks that the mothers’ right to bury their sons receive its own hearing.
Vale brings the written plea back to Teucer. He adds the completed household burial and signs the Trojan account for Dione. The paper now carries his own testimony.
Vale brings the written plea back to Teucer. He adds the completed public burial and signs the Trojan account for Dione. The paper now carries his own testimony.

Vale buries Ajax after Teucer’s appeal.
Vale buries Ajax beside Tecmessa and Eurysaces.
Vale buries Ajax while the camp looks on.
Vale deposits provisions and the witness tablet beside the boat. Helen accepts a witnessed passage agreement.
Vale deposits the witness tablet and agrees to carry the household's claim to a public hearing. No killing is authorized or recorded.
Vale digs Ajax’s grave with the camp tools.
Vale gives Dione Myrine’s signed return list. It names the bench, basket and berth Thaleia kept for the listed households. Dione keeps it at her table.
Vale gives Dione the Marathon record. Heracles’s daughter gave her life; Alcmene later ordered the captive Eurystheus to die. Dione keeps it at her table.
Vale gives Dione the funeral account from Eleusis. Evadne’s death and Iphis’s grief remain in the telling. Dione keeps it at her table.

Vale gives Thaleia the mothers’ list. She reserves the prepared bench, basket and next open berth for those households. Their names stay beside the mooring rope until they arrive.

Vale gives Theseus the mothers’ petition. He takes up the burial claim as the city’s own duty. The herald sets out for Thebes with a burial truce that names the dead, a return road and witnesses from both sides.
Vale gives the funeral urn to the mothers. They name their sons over the ashes. Aethra writes the funeral account and the households’ return list for Thaleia.
Vale lays the cloths from Piraeus beside Aethra. The mothers prepare the returned dead. Their children gather near the shrine while the funeral attendants carry out the rite.
Vale records Helen's request to remain under protection while the competing claims are heard.
Vale refuses to promise revenge while keeping the household’s testimony on record. Electra knows the answer.
Vale sets the filled jar beside Dione's table. She puts a loaf aside for Myrto's crew.
Vale sits with Aethra and the Argive mothers. Their sons died in the attack on Thebes. They ask Athens to recover the remains for burial. Aethra sets their petition and olive branch within reach.
Vale spreads the linen inside Ajax’s grave.
